title: An HSA Has Two Rulebooks: Getting Money In and Taking It Out
subtitle: Contribution eligibility and tax-free spending are separate tests. Keeping them separate can help you avoid costly assumptions and make better use of the balance you already have.
imageAlt: Two partners sit at a kitchen table reviewing separate health insurance cards, HSA statements and folders of medical receipts.
imageConcept: a couple of different ethnic backgrounds sharing a thoughtful moment together, in a specific visual scene about “An HSA Has Two Rulebooks: Getting Money In and Taking It Out”: A warm, documentary-style kitchen-table scene: two adults compare their own insurance cards and HSA records, with clearly separate folders and a shared notepad showing two columns, “Contributions” and “Expenses.”
body:
A Health Savings Account can look like one pot of money governed by one simple rule: have an HSA-eligible plan, then use the account for health costs. In practice, there are two different questions. Are you eligible to put money in for a particular month? And does a particular expense qualify for tax-free payment or reimbursement? The answers can differ. Losing the ability to contribute does not, by itself, make the existing balance unusable. An account holder can generally keep HSA funds in the account and use them tax-free for qualified medical expenses, while a distribution for a nonqualified expense is generally taxable and may also face an additional tax [1].

That distinction matters during a job change, a switch in insurance, enrollment in Medicare or a move onto a partner’s plan. It also matters when you’re sorting old receipts or deciding whether to pay a bill from savings instead of the HSA. Treat contribution eligibility and withdrawals as two separate checks—not as a single yes-or-no judgment about whether your HSA is “active.” These are federal rules; state tax treatment and plan-specific details may differ.
Rulebook one: contributions are about coverage and eligibility

For each month you want to contribute, check whether you meet the federal eligibility rules. In general, this involves having qualifying high-deductible health plan coverage and meeting other conditions, including rules about other health coverage, Medicare enrollment and whether someone else can claim you as a dependent. Eligibility is assessed month by month, so a change partway through the year can affect how much you may contribute without erasing money already in the account [1].

For 2026, the general HDHP standards include a minimum deductible of $1,700 for self-only coverage or $3,400 for family coverage, and maximum out-of-pocket amounts of $8,500 or $17,000, respectively. The annual HSA contribution limits are $4,400 for self-only coverage and $8,750 for family coverage [3]. Those figures are useful reference points, not a substitute for checking your actual plan and personal eligibility. Contribution limits can also depend on how many months you qualify and other applicable rules.

There are important 2026 exceptions to the assumption that only plans meeting the usual HDHP route can support HSA eligibility. IRS guidance addresses certain bronze and catastrophic plans and certain direct-primary-care arrangements [2]. If you are comparing coverage or making a contribution, confirm how your specific plan is treated under current rules; a plan label or deductible figure alone may not settle the question.
Rulebook two: withdrawals are about the expense

The account’s balance has a different test. To take money out tax-free, the distribution generally must pay or reimburse a qualified medical expense for the account holder, their spouse or an eligible dependent. The expense must have been incurred after the HSA was established. An expense does not become qualified simply because it is health-related, and an HSA distribution is not tax-free merely because you were eligible to contribute when you opened the account [1].

If a distribution is used for something that does not qualify, it is generally included in taxable income. An additional 20% tax may apply, with exceptions under federal law, including certain distributions after age 65, disability or death [1]. That means it is worth pausing before using the card for a borderline purchase. Check current IRS guidance or ask a qualified tax professional rather than relying only on a store’s “HSA eligible” label, a payment card approval or a remembered rule.

A change in coverage can therefore create a straightforward outcome: you may no longer be able to make new contributions for some months, while still holding an account whose existing funds can pay for eligible expenses. The two rulebooks answer different questions; one does not cancel the other.
Receipts are part of the tax benefit

An HSA’s tax advantages depend on being able to support how money was used. Keep records that identify the expense, its date, the amount and who received the care. Also keep evidence that it was not reimbursed by insurance or another source, and was not claimed as a tax deduction. The same expense cannot be used to support a tax-free HSA distribution and also claimed as a medical expense deduction [1].

A practical record might be a receipt paired with an explanation of the service, a payment confirmation and any insurance statement showing what was or was not reimbursed. Save digital copies in a place you can retrieve later, and keep them according to your broader tax-record practices. The aim is not to turn every routine purchase into paperwork; it is to preserve enough information to explain a distribution if questions arise.

Timing deserves attention, too. If you pay a qualifying bill from a regular checking account and plan to reimburse yourself later, keep the original documentation and confirm that the expense was incurred after the HSA was established. Do not assume that an old bill can be reimbursed just because the account now has enough money.
A two-column check for a job change or plan switch

Make a simple timeline before adding money or reimbursing yourself. In the first column, list each month of the year and the coverage and eligibility facts that applied: plan type, coverage tier, other coverage, Medicare status and any relevant change dates. Mark months you believe you were eligible to contribute, then verify the result against your plan documents and current IRS rules. If coverage changed during a month, don’t guess at the effect; confirm the applicable monthly rule.

In the second column, list each HSA distribution or planned reimbursement. Record the expense date, service or item, amount, account-holder or family member it relates to, receipt location and whether insurance or another source paid any portion. Flag missing records, uncertain eligibility or any possibility of a duplicate reimbursement. The columns are deliberately separate: a month with no contribution eligibility does not automatically disqualify an otherwise eligible expense, and an eligible contribution month does not make every purchase tax-free.

This worksheet is a financial-literacy tool, not a personalized tax calculation. If the entries point to a possible excess contribution, a nonqualified distribution or unclear coverage status, take the records to a tax professional, insurer or HSA trustee and ask a specific question.
Reviewing accounts together without merging them

Partners can do this review side by side, but should keep the ownership and records for each account clear. An HSA is an individual account; sharing a household does not make two accounts one joint account. Each person can list their own coverage history, contribution activity, distributions and receipts, then compare notes on shared family expenses to make sure the same bill has not been reimbursed twice.

Start by gathering insurance cards and plan materials, HSA statements, payroll contribution records and receipts. Each person fills in their own timeline and expense list. Then compare only where it helps: Did a coverage change affect one person or both? Was a family expense paid from one account, and is the documentation easy to find? Is there an unresolved question for the insurer or trustee? Keep a written note of who will follow up and what they need to verify.

This approach can be particularly useful when one partner changes jobs or joins the other’s coverage. It replaces a vague household assumption—“we’re covered, so we can contribute”—with a clear record of each person’s circumstances and each account’s transactions.

The useful habit is to pause at two decision points. Before contributing, check eligibility and the applicable limit for the relevant year and months. Before taking money out, check that the expense qualifies, was incurred after the HSA was established, and has not been reimbursed or claimed elsewhere. Save the evidence as you go rather than trying to reconstruct the year at tax time.

For 2026, the rules include changes and exceptions, so older explanations may not cover every plan type or arrangement [2]. Verify current federal guidance and ask your insurer or HSA trustee about plan-specific coverage questions. For state taxes, check your state’s treatment separately. This is educational information, not individualized tax, insurance or investment advice; where your records or eligibility are uncertain, a qualified professional can help you apply the rules to your situation.
